video.title: The Easiest Online Business to Start in 2026

summary: Chris Koerner reviews seven businesses built around white-labeled or add-on software, mostly using GoHighLevel, and explains how they target specific niches. He highlights recurring pricing, starting with a narrow feature, and building from knowledge of an industry’s problems. He also covers localized software opportunities, research tools, and a plugin model. His central caution is that one-time pricing can fail when ongoing platform, support, and acquisition costs outlast the customer payment.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Solo host presenting a listicle and business analysis.

ideas.name: Loan Signing System notary software
ideas.one_liner: A notary training business expanded into a niche CRM built on GoHighLevel.
ideas.business_model: Subscription software, with a separate course.
ideas.customer: Mobile notaries and loan signing agents.
ideas.problem: Notaries need a place to manage customer records, activity, and email.
ideas.offer: A niche CRM for notaries, alongside a course about the business.

pricing.model: Monthly or annual software subscription; separate course sale.
pricing.notes: The host says the software is built on GoHighLevel. Prices and customer-count claims are the host's account of the business.

acquisition_channels.details: The founder had trained notaries and knew the notary business before building software for that audience.

quote.text: And this dude's trained like a bunch of notaries. So he knew the notary business.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Software access to a CRM that tracks activity and customers and stores email records; the host says GoHighLevel provides the underlying software. A course is also sold.
unit_economics_claims: The host says the business has over 1,000 customers and estimates at least $100,000 monthly revenue from the software.
The host says a separate course costs about $400.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the host says the business began in 2024 and had been operating for about two years.

acquisition.how: Niche content and an existing notary audience could bring inbound leads, but building trust and finding partners still needs human work. The host also recommends unsolicited DMs, which are legally restricted in the UK.

onboarding.how: Account setup and CRM templates can be automated, with human help for niche-specific configuration.

delivery.how: CRM access and routine record management are software-delivered; the underlying platform is provided by GoHighLevel.

billing.how: Recurring subscription billing can run through software with occasional human oversight.

support.how: Basic support can use a knowledge base and automation, but account and workflow problems may need human help.

uk_applicability.notes: A niche CRM for UK notaries is feasible, subject to adapting workflows and support to UK notarial and loan-signing practices.

risks: The host recommends unsolicited social DMs and payment-service messages to individuals; UK rules restrict unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders.
The business relies on a third-party platform, so platform pricing, availability, and terms affect margins and continuity.
The host's revenue estimate is based on stated customer counts and subscription prices, not audited accounts.

tactics.name: Start with a niche you already understand
steps: Choose an industry where you have worked or run a service business.
List the recurring tasks, delays, and frustrations operators face.
Talk to people in that industry before choosing a software feature.
Build a focused solution for a problem they already recognize.

quote.text: They're starting with what they know, because they know the pain points.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Sell a narrow feature, then expand
steps: Unbundle one useful feature from a larger software product.
Use the feature to earn trust with one customer segment.
Add related software or CRM features as upsells after customers use the first product.

quote.text: Unbundle one little feature from a bigger piece of software. Sell that hard and then start giving them upsells and more and more software offerings.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Find product gaps in customer reviews
steps: Search G2 for software in a target niche.
Collect customer reviews and ask an AI tool to identify missing features users complain about.
Check whether the feature can be built as a GoHighLevel snapshot or add-on.
Validate that customers will pay before building a large product.

quote.text: If you don't have to do that, just ask chat JBT, help me build a go-high level snapshot from this.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Partner with an existing niche creator
steps: Find a creator with a focused audience in the target industry.
Offer to build software for the creator’s audience.
Propose a 50/50 split, as the host suggests.
The host recommends contacting them through social DMs or PayPal; in the UK, marketing DMs to individuals and sole traders generally require consent.

quote.text: build this for them, split it with them 50, 50, slide it into their DMs on Twitter, Strava, personal Facebook, Venmo, PayPal, anywhere that isn't crowded
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Study a business before copying its model
steps: Pick one company to study for a week.
Compare its current offer and pricing with older versions of its website in the Wayback Machine.
Check current reviews on G2 or Trustpilot for complaints and product gaps.
Use the Meta Ads Library and Google search to inspect its ads.
Research the founder and look for evidence of how the company operates.

quote.text: pick one and spend the next week studying them, studying their pricing, their website, their ads in the meta ads library, Google that.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Check recurring costs before choosing one-time pricing
steps: List recurring platform, support, advertising, and labour costs.
Compare those costs with the expected lifetime revenue per customer.
Use recurring pricing when customers receive ongoing access and support.
Do not rely on one-time payments unless acquisition and retention economics cover ongoing obligations.

quote.text: When you copy any one of these businesses, ask yourself, just my pricing cover, my high level bill, plus my time, plus my ads, plus my support every single month, forever.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Localize a proven software model
steps: Look for a language or country where businesses lack local CRM options.
Choose a market you can understand and support.
Translate snapshots and support documents with AI, then review them for accuracy.
Adapt pricing, integrations, and support to the local market.

tactics.name: Build retention into the product ecosystem
steps: Bundle training, software, coaching, and community around one customer workflow.
Keep related resources and relationships in the same product environment.
Make the product useful beyond the initial training purchase.
